title: Holy company
hook: Sikhs stress the company of the good

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan in the Sikh way: the Guru Granth Sahib sung, not just read. Your line was sung scripture. Did a song carry a line further into your day than words alone would have? Day one thousand four hundred two.

Shoes off at the door. Head covered. Inside a gurdwara, the hall is carpeted, and people sit on the floor facing the Guru Granth Sahib. A banker sits beside a taxi driver. A grandmother sits beside a student who came straight from the gym. Nobody has a better seat. Later, in the kitchen hall, they sit again, in rows on the floor, and are served the same simple meal by volunteers who may have been sitting next to them an hour ago. Who you sat with matters here, maybe more than how long you stayed. Sikhs have a word for the people in that room, and for what being among them does to a person.
screen: `SHOES OFF, HEAD COVERED.` → `NOBODY HAS A BETTER SEAT.` → `WHO YOU SAT WITH MATTERS.`

segments.voice: The word is sangat. It means company, the gathering, the congregation. At a gurdwara, the sangat is everyone who has come: the singers, the cooks, the visitors, you. Sikhs speak of the sadh sangat, the company of the holy, and the Guru Granth Sahib praises it. One whole section of the Sukhmani Sahib, a long hymn by Guru Arjan, praises that company line after line. In plain paraphrase: in the company of the holy, the face grows bright, the dirt on the mind is washed away, pride falls off, and the Name of God comes easily. Notice what the hymn is claiming. Not only that good people are pleasant to be around. It is claiming that company changes you. You become, a little, like the people you sit with. So for Sikhs, choosing your company is not a social detail. It is part of the practice, like rising early or singing the hymns. And the sangat is not a crowd you watch. It is a body you join. You sing with it, cook with it, sweep with it, sit in its rows to eat. The same word, sangat, shows up far from the gurdwara, too. A family might say the sangat helped them through a funeral. A visitor might be welcomed with: the sangat is your family now. Strip away the language and the question is a plain one, and sharp. Whose company makes you more patient, more honest, more like the person you mean to be? And whose company quietly pulls the other way? Sikhs answer the first part with a place and a people: come and sit with the sangat.
screen: `SANGAT: THE COMPANY, THE CONGREGATION.` · `SADH SANGAT: THE COMPANY OF THE HOLY.` · `COMPANY CHANGES YOU.` · `A BODY YOU JOIN, NOT A CROWD YOU WATCH.` · then, large: `COME AND SIT WITH THE SANGAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your good company. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one person in whose company you become a little better. Kinder, calmer, more honest. It might be a friend, a teacher, a grandparent, a neighbor. Hold their face for a moment. Notice what changes in you when you picture sitting next to them. Then, gently, ask when you last spent real time with them. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. If you don't, simply let yourself be glad they exist. The bell holds the time.
Sangat. The company, the congregation, in the Sikh tradition. Sadh sangat is the company of the holy, the people whose presence washes the mind. Today's word.
Your line: good company. Today, make one real plan to spend time with the person you pictured, a call, a walk, a meal. Sit beside them, even for a little while. Day one thousand four hundred two.

howItsDone: Sikhs gather as the sangat at the gurdwara to hear and sing the Guru Granth Sahib, then sit together in rows to share langar, a free meal served by volunteers; keeping good company is treated as part of spiritual life.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: the company, the congregation.

trapdoor: what you thought: sangat sounds like a crowd at a service.
what it means: the company of seekers, a body you join, and in the sadh sangat a company that changes you.
what a scholar hears: Guru Arjan's Sukhmani Sahib gives a whole section to praising the company of the holy, line after line.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtapadi 7 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 271–272)

notes: Sukhmani Sahib is paraphrased (no Macauliffe wording checked). Confirm that ashtapadi 7 is the section in praise of the saadh sang and that the paraphrased images (face made bright, mind's filth washed away, pride dispelled, the Name comes easily) fairly reflect it; confirm the Ang range 271–272.
The gurdwara scene (shoes off, heads covered, sitting on the floor, langar in rows served by volunteers) is described generally, without numbers or claims about all gurdwaras. Confirm.
The visitor greeting 'the sangat is your family now' is presented as something a person might say, not a fixed formula. Confirm it reads naturally.
